questions.q: Discuss disadvantages of the traditional file processing system. [10]
questions.model: Write all you can: Data redundancy. The same information is duplicated in several files (e.g. a student's name, roll number and class in both Library and Examinations). It raises storage and access cost.; Data inconsistency. Copies of the same data hold different values; changing a name in the library but not in exams leaves contradictions. Every file holding the item must be changed.; Accessing anomalies (difficulty in accessing data). Needed data cannot be retrieved conveniently or efficiently. Example: the bank officer who wants customers in zip code 600001, then only those with balance of 10,000 or more, needs a new program written each time because the request was not anticipated.; Data isolation. Data is scattered in many files, in different formats, so writing new programs to retrieve the right data is difficult.; Integrity problems. Consistency constraints (e.g. balance never below 500) are coded inside application programs; adding a new constraint means changing many programs.; Atomicity problems. After a failure the data must return to the consistent state before it. Example: transferring 50 from A to B; a crash can remove it from A without crediting B. The transfer must be all or nothing, which is hard in a file system.; Concurrent access anomalies. Many users update at the same time without coordination. Example: account A holds 500; withdrawals of 50 and 100 at about the same time can leave 450 or 400 instead of 350.; Security problems. Not every user should see all data. Programs are added ad hoc, so enforcing it is hard. Example: payroll staff should see employee data but not customer accounts.;

questions.q: Discuss advantages of a DBMS over the traditional file processing system. [10]
questions.model: The notes list 15 advantages (learn them all, then choose ten): Controlling Data Redundancy; Data Consistency; Data Sharing; Data Integration; Integrity Constraints; Data Security; Data Atomicity; Database Access Language; Development of Application; Creating Forms; Report Writers; Control over Concurrency; Backup and Recovery Procedures; Data Independence; Advanced Capabilities; Detail for each is in the Unit 1 notes in Part 4.

questions.q: Explain any five types of schedules with suitable example. [10]
questions.model: Know all seven; write any five: Serial schedule. No interleaving of operations of different transactions; always consistent. Example: T1 (R(A), A=A+50, W(A)) completes, then T2 (R(A), A=A+100, W(A)). A=100 gives 150 then 250; T2 then T1 also gives 250. Disadvantages: limits concurrency, wastes CPU, short transactions may wait long.; Complete schedule. The last operation of every transaction is commit or abort. Example: T1: R(A) W(A) Commit; T2: R(A) W(A) Abort.; Recoverable schedule. If Tj reads a value written by Ti, then Ti must commit before Tj. Example: T1: R(A), A=A+10, W(A), Commit; then T2: R(A), A=A-5, W(A), Commit.; Non-recoverable schedule. A transaction does a dirty read from an uncommitted transaction and commits before that transaction does. Example: T1 R(x) x=x+10 W(x); T2 R(x) x=x-5 W(x) Commit; T1 fails. T2 should be rolled back but has already committed.; Cascading schedule (cascading rollback). Failure of one transaction forces several dependent transactions to roll back or abort. Example: T1 writes A=A-50; T2 and T3 read that value; T1 fails, so T2 and T3 abort too.; Cascadeless schedule. A transaction may read a value only after the transaction that wrote it commits. Example: T1: R(A) W(A) Commit; then T2: R(A) W(A) Commit; then T3: R(A) W(A) Commit.; Strict schedule. A value written by a transaction cannot be read or overwritten by another transaction until the writer commits or aborts. Every strict schedule is recoverable and cascadeless. Example: T1: R(A) W(A) Commit; only then T2: W(A) R(A).; Also know: serializable (equivalent to a serial schedule; conflict or view), non-serial (operations interleaved). Strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable.

questions.q: Define concurrent execution of transaction. Explain the types of conflicts that may occur, with an example of each. [2+8=10]
questions.model: Concurrent execution means multiple transactions run concurrently in the DBMS, each doing its atomic unit of work. Advantages: decreased waiting time, improved throughput and resource utilisation. Problems (conflicts) follow. Lost update (write-write, W-W). Two transactions access the same item and their operations interleave so the item ends up wrong. Example: x=100. T1 reads 100, adds 10; T2 reads 100, subtracts 20; T1 writes 110; T2 writes 80. T1's update is overwritten (correct serial result would be 90).; Dirty read / temporary update (write-read, W-R). A transaction updates an item and then fails (not committed), but another transaction has already read the uncommitted value. Example: x=100; T1 writes x=110; T2 reads 110 and writes 160; T1 fails. T2 used a value that never existed.; Incorrect summary. One transaction computes an aggregate (e.g. a sum) while another updates some of the records, so the aggregate mixes old and new values. Example: A=100, Y=200; T2 sums A (100) then reads Y; T1 changes Y to 300 in between. The sum is wrong.; Unrepeatable read (read-write, R-W). T1 reads an item twice and T2 changes it between the two reads, so T1 sees two different values. Example: A=1000; T1 reads 1000; T2 writes A=3000; T1 reads again and gets 3000.;
